en: The Eighth Great Section of the *Shi Dunlun Jizhuan Lunben*, Part Eighty-Eight:
Explaining the Knowledge of Affairs, etc. First, the four lines of verse are listed; these constitute four [sections].
Section on the Gate. In the prose commentary, the first part explains the gate of the knowledge of affairs (*karmāntajñāna*):
although the two types of knowledge—erroneous and correct—take the same object as their cognitive focus, they differ in that one involves grasping while the other does not.
When right knowledge arises,
it does not destroy the object of that false knowledge;
rather, it merely abandons the false attachment toward that very object.
The second explains the transformation of the practices of pleasure and so forth;
the third explains the teaching of the sutra whether requested or unrequested.
Both may be understood according to the text.
The fourth [section] explains nirvāṇa in two ways:
first, it distinguishes complete nirvāṇa;
second, it clarifies partial nirvāṇa.
Regarding the preceding section,
Master Jing says that "conforming instruction" refers to the "prophetic declaration," which is precisely the wheel of mind-reading.
Instruction refers to the wheel of verbal instruction through the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*).
Miraculous manifestation refers to...
This is the wheel of supernormal power of the body.
It is the Tathāgata’s ability to provide a prophetic declaration regarding the minds of others according to his wish, even extending to minds that have ceased long ago through successive transitions;
that is, regarding minds already extinguished over immeasurable and vast kalpas in the past.
If there is one who has extinguished the mind in this world,
then all the minds that existed in their immediately preceding lives,
as well as the minds that currently operate upon objects in the present— [all these would likewise be extinguished].
Regarding the mind that arises during the present lifetime:
from the moment one has emerged from meditative concentration until the point where it does not rely on a single moment—

this explains the preceding [discussion of] the mind that has long since ceased due to conditions and the mind that has ceased immediately prior, provided that the mind now turns toward a present object.
Furthermore, this is based on the category as a whole and not on individual moments,
as has already been explained previously.
The Tathāgata possesses no unconcentrated mind.
As for the statement that "having arisen from meditative concentration,
one engages in subsequent recollective discrimination," this is said because [the practitioner] shares characteristics with the two vehicles. Thus,
the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) comprehensively knows the three periods of time, knowing multiple minds and mental factors (caitta) simultaneously.

This differs from the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) of the two vehicles, which only takes the present as its object and perceives only the mind-king (*cittarāja*), without knowing its numerical attributes and other such qualities.
Master Bei said:
"In this text, since the knowledge of others' minds already knows the past, how does it differ from the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*)?"
The commentary states:

If one knows the limits of mental phenomena (*cittadharma*), it is called the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*); if one knows the limits of various objective matters (*vastu*), it is called the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*).
Furthermore, at the time of the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the knowledge of others' minds, one desires to know the mind.
Regarding the desire to know all matters through the skillful means of past lives (*pūrvajanma-upāya*), the Master Da says:
"Furthermore, based on the three dharmas... and so forth.
This is a further explanation of the three preceding sections on the "Conformity to Instruction" and so forth.
Below, the partial nirvāṇa is elucidated.
Master Da says:
Because it resembles nirvana, it is called "partial nirvana" (tad-aṃśa-nirvāṇa).
It is like food and drink when one is hungry and thirsty;
this is termed "minor nirvana."
The Ninth Great Gate: Explaining Disputes and so forth.
First, the verse lists seven gates:
first, disputes (*adhikaraṇa*).
2. Sprout; 3.
Seeing great defilement;
4. Single destination.
The five trainings;
the six terrors;
the latter half of the verse constitutes the seventh section.
In the prose commentary, the section on "disputes" is first explained.
Regarding the term *āśīla*,
it is a proper name for a specific individual.
Regarding "Mātanga":
a woman of the Caṇḍāla caste is named Mātangī;
a man of the Caṇḍāla caste is named Mātaṅga.
These two are common names.
This woman makes her living merely by sweeping with a cloth,
yet worldly people falsely designate her as being of great wealth and great riches.
The Tathāgata, following that [explanation], also speaks of "great wealth.
In the second section, the "Gate of Explaining the Sprout," there is first a general heading.
Next is the brief explanation,
followed by the detailed analysis.
Within the brief explanation, the single cause is first distinguished.
The latter clarifies the two conditions.
Master Jing says:
"As for the practitioner of the five grades..."
First, the intrinsic nature of all conditioned phenomena;
second, the causes and conditions of all conditioned phenomena;
third, the cause of affliction.
The four are the causes of purification;
the fifth is purification itself.
These five constitute the purifications.
Among these five, the causal condition for defilement consists of the seeds of the afflictions;
they follow along with the ālayavijñāna as the cause and take the four stations of consciousness as the condition.
Furthermore, because craving and attachment moisten karma, causing the sprout to continue its succession,
they are called "conditions. Master Da (達師) and others state that the five aggregates themselves are what are termed the "five categories" (*pañcavastuka*).
In the *Liaojian*, it says:
"Regarding the statement that 'in this case, there is one who will never again be born,' this person currently creates new karma and causes [old karma] to increase."
Later, having become an Arhat, he causes the seeds to rot so that no sprouts can grow.
As for the statement, "Furthermore, there is one who... until later on, even sprouts cannot grow," it refers to this.
According to the completion of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*),
or according to the [periods of] one hundred or sixty kalpas and so forth,
one is capable of attaining the eight higher fruits within the present body.
This causes the sprout not to arise.
Furthermore, there is another who dwells on the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) and will not be born again;
although their births in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) have been exhausted, they still remain in the higher realms.
Regarding the statement, "In contrast to this, it should be known that all those with the sprout of existence attain growth":
this refers to those who are the opposite of the three types of persons mentioned above;
namely, the external ordinary beings whose sprout of existence grows.
Third, the explanation of seeing the great defilement.
Master Jing says:
first, seeing; second, the remaining afflictions.
Those who perceive defilement conceive of "I" and "mine," and thus take up other [views];
these constitute the fundamental basis for all those among the outsiders who pursue various paths.
The other four types of views and the sixty-two views have the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their root;
the remaining afflictions constitute the second type of defilement.
Furthermore, when one is liberated from the defilement of views, one is also liberated from the others, whereas when one is liberated from the others, one is not necessarily liberated from the views.

Why is this? Because among those born therein, there are those who, relying on the worldly path, have attained liberation up to the point of being free from craving for the sphere of nothingness, yet remain unliberated from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Thus, while cultivation is suppressed, views are not;
furthermore, both the afflictions of view and those of cultivation can be abandoned.

Because of these views, one does not discern the differences among the various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) belonging to the lower and higher stages, which are mixed together in their own-being, but instead reckons them collectively as "self" or as "belonging to a self."
This passage explains the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
It holds that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) across the nine stages are collectively regarded as being caused by the self.
On the supramundane path, one first abandons the view of a personal body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and subsequently and permanently abandons the remaining afflictions (*kleśa*).
Therefore, it is said that "only seeing the afflictions (*saṃkleśa*) is the great affliction.
Regarding the realization of the teacher,
it is stated that all afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) are called "afflictions of seeing" (*darśana-saṃkleśa*).
All afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation are termed "remaining afflictions.
With the exception of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
the remaining four views are termed "various external views."
Since this text states that one has not yet escaped the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
we know that by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) one only suppresses the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanākleśa*) but does not suppress the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭikleśa*).

Furthermore, it says that regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) belonging to the lower and higher stages, one perceives their mixed nature as a single entity without observing their distinctions.
Thus, one should know that according to the Mahāyāna doctrine, the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) also takes both its own stage and other stages as its object;
however, it takes them collectively rather than individually.
Furthermore, when one’s own body resides in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), one can only take the higher stages as objects.
Therefore, the preceding passage states, "arising from this.
However, no textual passage is seen that describes the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) arising in a higher stage taking a lower stage as its object.
Examine the subsequent passage yourself.
Desire is like [the view of self] as it arises in higher realms, taking the dharmas of lower realms as "self.
Therefore, by collectively reckoning these three as "self" or as "belonging to self," one may ascend even to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) and yet subsequently fall back.
The Tripiṭaka Master says: "When the body is born in a higher stage, the body also takes the phenomena of a lower stage as its object, regarding them as 'self.
This is as stated in the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*: the craving of a higher stage takes a lower stage as its object."
This is also like that.
One should understand that the fourth [meaning] is "one destination" (ekāyana).
The path is called "one destination" by virtue of three characteristics.
This means that on the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*), one observes all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) by means of five modes of practice.
Thus, these conditioned phenomena are cultivated and purified during two periods:
namely, during the stage of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*) and the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa-bhūmi*).
The preceding section on ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) establishes the three characteristics.
The question "What are called the five practices? (*pañca-caryā*) below introduces the five practices individually.
The Master Da said:
"As for the 'five locations,' they refer to the five aggregates (skandhas)."
As for "intrinsic nature," it refers to the intrinsic nature of all contaminated conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
As for "the causes and conditions of conditioned phenomena,"...
It refers to the causal conditions that, being subsumed under the Truth of Origination, bring about the Truth of Suffering.
As for the causal conditions of affliction,
they are the sensation of joy.
The causes and conditions for purification are the afflictions;
"purification" refers to [the state free from them].
This is the Truth of Cessation that has been attained.
Fifth is the explanation of the trainings (*śikṣā*).
Master Jing’s commentary states:

As for the statement, "What are the five modes of contemplation? They are: contemplating all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the causes and conditions of conditioned phenomena, the causes and conditions of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), the causes and conditions of purification (*vyavadāna*), and cessation and tranquility," this combines the preceding five [modes] into one.
Because it leads toward the path of purification and liberation,
it is precisely the aforementioned cause of purification;
for all conditioned phenomena possess a manifold and diverse nature.
Regarding the phrase "the first [category], the intrinsic nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
because each arises from its own seed," this provides a detailed explanation of the cause.
"Each arises depending on other conditions" distinguishes the conditions (*pratyaya*) of the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);
the latter two [phrases] together explain the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) of the conditioned phenomena.
The Master Da says that as for the "five locations," they are as previously described; herein,
there are five distinct modes of manifestation.
The first differentiated aspect consists of summarizing the aforementioned five aspects.
The second aspect is that of tending toward the path of purification and liberation.
Because it assists in accomplishing the first mode of activity (*ākāra*),
the first mode of activity attains pure transcendence (*nairyāṇika-viśuddhi*).
Third, because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) possess a manifold and diverse nature, this is the third mode of activity.
This characteristic further explains and establishes the intrinsic nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Because each arises from its own respective seed,
this is the fourth characteristic.
It further establishes that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have causes and conditions as their basis,
because each of the five arises in dependence upon other conditions;
this is the fifth aspect.
This provides a general explanation that the preceding four lines arise through dependent origination.
There is an interpretation which states:
"In general, the five aggregates are summarized as the Four Noble Truths."
First is the truth of suffering,
which refers to the initial conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Second is the truth of origination.
Then the next two [truths] are the objects of the second stage;
the third, the truth of cessation,
is the object of the fourth stage.
Because one attains purity through the cessation and tranquility of conditions.
The treatise states, "because of cessation and tranquility";
the meaning lies therein.
The Truth of the Path is the fifth aspect;
since the path itself is pure,
it is able to bring about purification and cessation.
The final three phrases provide a further explanation.
The first phrase explains the aforementioned "all conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāra*),
while the latter two phrases explain the causes and conditions of those formations.
The sixth [section] explains the four fears.
Master Jing’s commentary states:
"Due to four causes and conditions, fear arises in two locations and acts as an obstacle."
First, they feel fear toward conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);
second, they feel fear toward nirvāṇa.
Because they give rise to such fear, they do not experience joy in the Noble Teaching or in nirvāṇa.
It is called an "obstruction.
It is due to four factors:
first, the arising of fear regarding one's status.
First, it refers to the arising of fear while in the state of one who is not noble.
Second, it refers to the arising [of fear] based on this dharma,
namely, by reckoning the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as "I" or "mine" and taking them as a basis.
Hearing the teaching on non-self, one gives rise to fear.
Third, as for "arising in this way," it means that fear arises due to the two kinds of transformation and disintegration of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
First, that which is corrupted by external conditions refers to the arising of fear due to favorable or unfavorable conditions, such as the conditions of old age or illness.

Second, that which is corrupted by the mind’s own arising of false discrimination refers to the arising of fear within a single object due to the mind’s false conceptualization of whether it exists or does not exist, or whether it is permanent or impermanent.
Fourth, regarding the arising of the aspects of conduct (*caryā-nimitta*):
this refers to the aspect of fear arising from the anxiety that what is cherished will undergo transformation and decay,
and the aspect of affliction (*kleśa*) arising when it is actually undergoing transformation and decay, and so forth.
Thus far, it has always been the first [type of fear]:
the arising of fear toward conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), as well as the mode of fear consisting in the conceptualization of nirvāṇa itself as the permanent disintegration of one's own being.
When such characteristics of activity manifest in their various forms,
one fails to develop affection for the sublime teaching or a longing for nirvāṇa;
this is called the obstruction of the two bases.
Furthermore, by way of two doors, the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self proceeds with distinctions regarding the objects of focus and one's own sphere of activity:
that which investigates is view,
and that which experiences is feeling.
There is an interpretation:
herein, the five modes of observation—namely, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), their causes, conditions, and so forth—are called the "five bases.
The seventh [section] explains the distinctions between well-spoken and ill-spoken teachings, as well as the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*).
Master Jing’s commentary explains:
herein, first, based on evil teachings, one calculates permanence and impermanence;
with regard to wholesome teachings, it is not so.
Next, based on erroneous teaching, one does not know suffering as it truly is and thus gives rise to a relish for it;
consequently, one develops attachment toward and longing for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the three periods of time respectively,
and is unable to cultivate disenchantment or dispassion.
The one who skillfully teaches the Dharma is the opposite of that.
Third, the one who poorly teaches the Dharma:
such wrong conduct is defiled by the four stains and can induce further results; through the dominant power of these two types [of causes], as described below...
The reasons for their exclusion or inclusion can be understood from the specific explanation of the underlying causes of views (*dṛṣṭi*), conceit (*māna*), and craving (*rāga*).
Regarding the statement that "not comparing oneself with others among the various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is called 'view' (*dṛṣṭi'), while comparing oneself is called 'pride' (*māna'),
and such false attachments belong to the category of ignorance (*avidyā*)," this explains that views and pride are collectively designated as ignorance.
Taking this as the precursor, one gives rise to craving and attachment, which belong to the category of "thirst" (*tṛṣṇā*).
It is by means of these two fundamental afflictions that one wanders incessantly through the cycle of birth and death.
Ignorance is the initial condition for the beginning [of existence],
and craving is the final condition for its beginning;
therefore, birth and death are not severed.
"This is well-spoken, for it can sever the four kinds of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
Master Da said:
"Although there are still other afflictions... and so forth.
This explains away the anticipated objection. An opponent objects:
"Since there are immeasurable afflictions (*kleśa*), why are only these three—view, pride, and craving—designated as the defilement of affliction?"
To provide a brief explanation of this general principle:
although other afflictions exist, these three alone are singled out for mention because they are the most preeminent and powerful.
From "those afflictions" onwards,
there is a detailed and general refutation of objections.
Furthermore, within this section, from "view and the conceit of self" onwards...
The tenth major section, "Explaining 'Insatiability' and Other Terms," which analyzes the various distinctions among names within the sūtras,
presents eight topical headings in verse.
First, freedom from weariness and desire;
second, freedom from confused questioning and explanation;
third, the characteristics.
Four obstacles,
five wonders,
and six causes.
Seventh, disparagement;
eighth, subsequent to that which is purely defiled.
In the prose commentary, the first explains "absence of desire."
First, the primary exposition on the absence of weariness with desire;
furthermore, there is weariness with desire.
Second, the explanation of answering questions without confusion.
Regarding the initial general presentation of the two types,
the subsequent section provides a detailed explanation of those two.
Within the former [section]:
If there are those with pure faith who inquire with a good heart,
or various non-Buddhists who come to inquire— whether with malicious intent or otherwise—
one should separately distinguish between these two types.
First, there is the "Record Distinguishing Non-confusion Based on the Question Concerning Arising and Ceasing";
second, there is the "Record Distinguishing Non-confusion Based on the Question Concerning the Holy Life.
Within the former, it refers to those who rely upon the Middle Way.
This is answered by way of the Middle Way.
Regarding the question of whether, during the arising and ceasing of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), there is no increase in sentient beings nor decrease in substantial entities:
it is not the case that one superimposes the existence of a truly real sentient being as being the actual arising and ceasing.
Because sentient beings are conventionally designated and lack any substantial essence,
one can discern the phenomena of arising and ceasing through causes and conditions;
they exist as illusions, possessing both birth and cessation.
One must not dismiss [the teaching] by saying that the law of dependent origination is without arising and without cessation, for such would constitute the error of nihilism (apavāda).
Rather, one should provide an account that establishes arising and cessation within all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) without confusion.
From here below, it clarifies the departure from the two extremes.
Regarding the second section, which distinguishes the unconfused answer concerning the inquiry into the holy life (*brahmacarya*),
Master Jing says:
Or if someone later asks, "For what reason and by what causes do you practice the holy life under the śramaṇa Gautama?
you should say, "It is because of Upavāṇa."
If one attains this level of questioning, it is called "answering without confusion.

For instance, someone might ask: "For what reason, among the many śramaṇas, do you specifically single out the names of the Vāsmaraputra and others to declare that they are practicing the holy life (brahmacarya)?"
"Does he not mention the names of others?
If one receives this question,
one should answer as previously stated.
If one does not mention the name of even a single person among the assembly, it will be unclear which group is being described as practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*),
and thus the discourse would be deficient. Conversely,
if one were to describe the names of all other śramaṇas in detail, it would become excessively prolix.
This would then constitute an unwarranted addition (*samāropa*).
Now, when one calls a single name for all others,
it is free from both addition and subtraction (*apavāda*).
If one claims that sentient beings can cultivate defilement and purity, this is called "increase";
to say that there is no cultivation at all is called "decrease.
To cultivate for the sake of wearying detachment from and the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is what is termed the Middle Way.
There is another interpretation:
that which is called "Gautama" is the old name for "Kauṭṭhāna."
This is the lineage of the Buddhas.
If someone asks, "For what reason do you practice the holy life under the Buddha?
and one receives this question, one should answer by means of the Middle Way.
This means that one does not superimpose the existence of real sentient beings while practicing defilement and purification,
nor does one deprecate them by asserting that they do not exist at all.
This is the third explanation of the characteristics.
Conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are said to have three characteristics.
Regarding the characteristic of "difference" (anyathātva):

as long as one has not died, the similar types [of phenomena] undergo arising and ceasing in every moment; because they are distinct from moment to moment, it is called the characteristic of difference.
Regarding transformation into a different nature:
it is as when, after death, one arises from that which possesses faculties to that which lacks faculties.
This is the fourth explanation of obstacles.
First, the distinction between hindrance and non-hindrance is clarified;
second, the characteristics of the noble ones are explained.
Within this, the two characteristics are first elucidated.
First, the faculties eliminate hindrances;
second, one receives the Buddha's prophecy.
Next, the three characteristics are explained.
Master Jing said:
"From 'by means of two kinds of characteristics' up to 'I have already fully understood,' [it means that] one now encounters a Noble One."
Regarding the prediction [of enlightenment] through three characteristics, it should be said that for noble beings there are two types:

namely, the two aforementioned characteristics of noble beings—first, the perfection of the lineage (*gotra*), and second, those who have merely completed their life span after being predicted and so forth.
The following is an explanation of the scriptural text.
Regarding "the Dharma that accords with the Dharma":
"Dharma" refers to the Noble Path preceded by right view.
"Following the Dharma" means relying upon the mental attentions (*manasikāra*) derived from hearing and reflecting on it.
Furthermore, "I have never disturbed the locus of the True Dharma" refers to the Blessed One,
for the Blessed One is the locus of the True Dharma.
The straightforward path would have been for him to say, "I have never troubled the World-Honored One.
Master Da said:
"He merely recorded the categories of things."
As stated in another sutra, the Buddha answered the question of where Upatiṣya would be reborn after his death.
Regarding the term "Upatiṣya," it means "one of a class" (or "a type of being").
There is an interpretation of the three characteristics herein:
first, the dharma;
second, that which conforms to the dharma.
Third, the basis for not disturbing the True Dharma.
Fifth, the explanation of marvelous phenomena (*āścaryadharma*).
Briefly, there are two kinds.
First, it causes those who have not yet gained faith to gain faith, and causes those who already possess faith to increase it.
Second, it enables one to swiftly attain realization and entry into the sublime teaching.
Regarding the phrase "virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end":
This refers to the first of the seven types of wholesomeness explained in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, namely the "wholesomeness of the present time.
It is called the second distinction because it specifies the two distinct periods of the present and the past.
The present is called "this world" (iha),
while the past is called "the other" (amutra).
This refers to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) in contrast to what precedes it.
Because it pertains to the higher realms and other worlds,
it is called the second distinction.
The sixth [point] explains the absence of a cause.
Regarding the statement "by way of two kinds of characteristics":
first, because of not understanding the causes and conditions for arising;
second, because of not understanding the causes and conditions for cessation.
Regarding the seventh [section], the explanation of "corruption":
first, the corruption is explained;
subsequently, the two types of ignorance that lead to its cessation are explained.
Regarding the former,
there are briefly two types:
first, merely using words to praise oneself and disparage others.
Second, although there is no praise or blame regarding the correct practice of preaching the Dharma, it is in truth praising oneself and disparaging others.
This is the eighth section on the subsequent gate concerning the defilement of understanding.
Master Jing said:
Regarding the eleven characteristics:
these five aggregates constitute five;
furthermore, by adding one downward [characteristic], there is the sixth.
Furthermore, following the [discussion on] defilement and purification, there are two additional characteristics,
which, added to the preceding, total eight. Moreover,
by means of three further characteristics, they are added to the preceding to total eleven.
One may also understand that regarding the three periods of time, there are eleven types of categories— internal and external, coarse and subtle, good and bad, far and near—
and so forth; masters such as Dashi and others have merely expounded the latter interpretation.
Chapter Eleven: Explanation of Dwelling with Few Desires and Other Qualities.
First, the verses list eighteen categories:
first, few desires (*alpeccha*).
Regarding the second [category], intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth, there are three gates;
regarding the third, the "recorded" (*vyākṛta*), there are likewise three gates.
Thus, the first phrase consists of eight gates.
The ninth is that which resembles the True Dharma;
the tenth is the locus of doubt and delusion;
the eleventh is the unrecorded.
12. Transformation and decay;
13. The Great Teacher’s prophecy;
14. Fulfillment of the three views.
Regarding the fifteen external marks of folly, at the end of the phrase "etc. (ādi), there are again three sections.
In the prose commentary, the first explains the three marks of dwelling with few desires.
When the Tathāgata’s mind enters into dwelling in fewness of desires,
abandoning affairs and manifesting the realization of principle,
this is called "fewness of desires in persons."
First, because the task has been completed;
second, because the disciples have already become weary of their practice;
and third, in order to transform those engaged in many worldly activities so that they may cultivate few desires.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the Tathāgata enters the peaceful divine abode (*śānta-divyavihāra*) as previously explained," this refers to what was stated in the eightieth-sixth fascicle:
that by means of eight causes and conditions, the Tathāgata enters the peaceful divine abode, and so forth, as explained at length.
Second is the explanation of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Master Jing says:
"There are, in brief, four kinds of natures of those to be converted who are to be disciplined."
The total number is four,
yet only three are listed;
one can thus see that the enumeration was mistaken.
The manuscript also contains an error;
it should be changed to "three.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation.
"Folly and negligence" constitute the first two [of the four].
Regarding the third, it is explained that by generating reverence toward the four points, one dwells [in them] and swiftly realizes the Unsurpassed.
Master Jing said:
The essential nature of reverence (*gaurava*) is not explicitly defined [in the sūtras].
According to the Hīnayāna, it is explained as affection (*preman*) and respect (*satkāra*).
Affection is faith (*śraddhā*).
Reverence is gradual.
Now, in this context, we investigate the terminology;
it appears that faith and desire are taken as the essence of reverence.
The Master Da said:
"Because one can give rise to the aspect of reverence within these four places,
there are thus four aspects."
Regarding the "four bases," this refers to what is stated below: "In that which is attained.
This is the fourth explanation of the three unsurpassed [qualities].
Master Jing said:
"In this context, the 'abiding in happiness in the present life' through wisdom and abandonment refers to the supremacy of wisdom."
The abandonment [of defilements] is the liberation through immovability of the mind (*āniñjya-cetovimukti*).
The path of swift progress characterized by bliss is the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).

As for the statement, "One should know that all practices of Arhats are designated as the path of swift progress characterized by bliss, and so forth": [this refers to the fact that they have abandoned the five lower fetters].
Based on this latter interpretation,
one understands that the aforementioned "unexcelled correct practice" refers to the "swift attainment of bliss";
that is, it designates the practice of all arhats by the name "swift attainment of bliss."
It is not by reference to the [four] elements that the four modes of practice are distinguished.
Master Da also said:
"The four tracks of practice possessed by this body of an Aśaikṣa are collectively termed the 'path of swift and pleasant progress'."
This is because they are not designated as "pleasant with slow realization," "pleasant with quick realization," "painful with slow realization," and so forth.
The following explains the reason:
it is said that "all coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) has been eternally extinguished" and "all that was to be done has been accomplished."
The fifth [point] is the correct understanding of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) during two periods.
Master Jing says:
"During two periods" means...
The first gate is by way of four kinds of characteristics;
this is the second gate.
One immediately realizes the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (āsrava-kṣaya) during these two occasions;
this is the third gate.
Next, the sequential explanation follows.
What are the two times?
First, while still on the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*),
that is, prior to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), an inner worldling (*adhyātma-prthagjana*) practices the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*).
One thoroughly understands that the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is a perverted grasping.
Regarding these two [types], during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
one abandons the conceptualized view of a self within the path of seeing.
Regarding the phrase "because of its intrinsic nature" up to "or as my possession":
this refers to conceiving a self and what belongs to a self (*ātman-ātmīya*) within the activity of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
As for "location," it refers to the objective referent (*ālambana-viṣaya*).
Regarding the object of focus, it is the false imputation of a self within that which is selfless.
As for its origination, it refers to craving conditioned by feeling, which arises from contact associated with ignorance and is comprised within [wrong] views.
It clarifies that [wrong view] originates from the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its root;
next, it gives rise to the sphere of views.
It clarifies that the aforementioned view of a self-body consists of regarding what is not superior as superior.
When associated with the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*),
there subsequently arises ignorance as a condition;
from feeling as a condition, craving arises— such are these phenomena.
Furthermore, [the view of self-identity] arises from that which is originated by the view of self-identity;
conversely, the view of self-identity may also arise from those [other views].
That is to say, by means of the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), one regards what is not superior as superior with respect to a self.
With ignorance and contact as conditions, feeling arises.
Feeling apprehends a self, and from that self arises craving for a self.
Because of this craving for a self, the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) arises, resulting in the firm attachment to a self.
Furthermore, there are five stages in the sequence of dependent origination, namely: "with the diversity of elements as condition, there arises the diversity of contact," and so forth.
Here, "elements" refers to the six elements;
these are equivalent to the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) being the conditions for contact.
Contact conditions feeling;
feeling conditions craving;
craving conditions grasping, and so forth.
Regarding the point "by way of the fruit," up until the time one investigates the dharma through the patience of non-self based on a single support,
this refers to the period prior to the path of seeing when one observes that there is no person in the dharma;
it also refers to the time of the two types of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
This refers to the stage of the path of vision (darśanamārga),
the three [stages of] attainment, and the time of becoming an Arhat;
these are the three periods enumerated here.

In this regard, at one time, due to the power of those latent tendencies—the view of a self-entity (satkāyadṛṣṭi)—there is delusion and doubt, even to the point of thinking, "I shall sever [this]," yet they do not incline toward entering [the path].
This is an obstacle for those prior to the path of seeing.
Even if they later transcend this and purify their minds, and have already attained the direct realization of the Noble Truths, [they remain obstructed].
These four roots of goodness have already attained a semblance of the direct realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), yet they have not yet attained the true path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
Within this stage, conceptualizations such as the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) and pride (*māna*) still arise, acting as obstacles to the path of vision.
This is the obstacle within the second stage.

While in the first two stages it is able to act as an obstacle through the power of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), in the third stage it is able to act as an obstacle through the power of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
First interpretation:
This conforms to the principle that is similar to the Hīnayāna,
which does not state that there are innate views of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and pride (*māna*) during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

There remain only the seeds of the habitual tendencies of the view of self and pride that are abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*), along with their manifest activity which acts as an obstruction; in the first two stages, these are termed "latent dispositions" (*anuśaya*).
Second, the explanation according to the gate of the actual principle (*yathārtha-naya*):

In the first two stages, because the manifest arising of conceptual views of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), pride (*māna*), and so forth acts as an obstacle, they are termed "latent dispositions" (*anuśaya*); this is because they function as the meaning of "proclivities" (*paryavasthāna*).
The third [type of] innate view and conceit that arises is called "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*).
It is named a habitual tendency because it arises based on the previously mentioned conceptualized views and conceits.
Furthermore, there are three conditions by which all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) grow and develop.
The commentary states that the formations of maturation arise from three conditions.

Alternatively, regarding the statement "the formations of afflictions," one who possesses pervasive knowledge of the stage of maturation understands the false faults of conceptualization, views, and pride.
Regarding the statement that "within the stage of seeing (darśana-bhūmi), one can attain the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (āsrava) to be abandoned by the path of seeing,
and subsequently, by abandoning the remaining fetters, one attains arhatship and so forth"—
this explains the third chapter.
At those two moments, one immediately realizes the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).
Master Tai stated:
"Some explain that this refers to the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), where one has not yet abandoned the intellectually acquired (*vikalpaja*) conceit (*asmimāna*)."
The Tripitaka Master did not permit it.
Master Da said, "In this context,
from 'at one time' up to 'not entering into the stream,' [the meaning is as follows]."
The section beginning with "At another time" explains the second [stage],
the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), following the explanation of the time of subduing and abandoning within the first application (*prayoga*).
Furthermore, following the section on the Noble Truths below,
there is another explanation regarding the third attainment— the time of becoming an Arhat—
extending even to the point where one no longer takes pleasure in entering [the cycle of existence].
This concludes the explanation of the first period.
From the passage "At another time" onwards, it explains the stages of seeing and cultivation.
Regarding the statement that "in the third stage, one is able to create obstacles through the power of habitual tendencies":
This refers to the third [category], which possesses only the obstacle of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The sixth [section] provides an explanation of the five characteristics and raises questions;
this is the first of the three gates recorded within the verse.
Regarding "by way of intrinsic nature," one should know that the fivefold intrinsic nature of form and so forth refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Regarding "by way of cessation," it means that among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), only the acquisition of desire and greed (*kāmarāga-prāpti*) is subject to total extinction.
This clarifies the abandonment of grasping for desire.
The following passage resolves the objection:
"Because that [grasping] cannot project [a future existence] in the present."
Because they are unable to project karmic formations toward their present bodies,
it is established that formations are of only two kinds: first,
those that create karma for future existence within the midst of a birth-result.
Regarding the second [category], it refers to the karma that produces future existence (*punarbhava*) within the context of later retribution;
thus, it is said there are "two kinds.
As for the "distinctions of categories," this refers to the eleven types [of karma] and so forth. Regarding their "origination" (*samutthāna*):
These are the five gates, beginning with the equality of the three periods of time.
Furthermore, regarding the "expedient means of transmigration," which refers to the categories of ignorance and craving according to their respective applications,
this is a further explanation of transmigration.
Because ignorance gives rise to the moisture of craving, it is said to "accord accordingly.
Furthermore, from the passage beginning with "due to two conditions" onwards,
the process of transmigration is explained again.
The seventh [section] explains the true record concerning the three locations;
this is the recorded answer to the second question among the three gates.
Master Jing said:

Regarding these three points, only the noble ones (ārya) provide true declarations, whereas ordinary beings (pṛthagjana)—except for those who have heard it from another—cannot do so because their views of a self or what belongs to a self among the conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are not in accordance with reality.
However, even though they are ordinary beings, those who have heard from another that "the self is not in accordance with reality" are indeed able to declare this.
If that [self-view] serves as the basis for the arising of the conceit "I am," this constitutes one section of the treatise; that is to say,
it distinguishes how self-view and the conceit "I am" function such that the conceit "I am" arises based upon self-view.
This refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Although they have already abandoned [other forms of self-view], this conceit of "I" (*asmimāna*) remains entirely unsevered;
thus, while their conceptualized view of a self (*vikalpa-ātma-dṛṣṭi*) has subsided, [the conceit persists].
This conceit born of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) remains entirely unsevered for those on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
This is the second gate.
If it is an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) basis of conceit that is not severed and thus continues to manifest as before:
Because the pride arising from innate satkāyadṛṣṭi still arises in noble ones (ārya) as it does not depend on conceptualized satkāyadṛṣṭi;
therefore, if it did not arise, the pride of "I am" (asmimāna) would not be abandoned and would continue to manifest as before.
It should be understood that within this context there are two kinds of *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am").
First, the *vikalpa-asmimāna* (conceptual conceit), which consists of attachment to the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that has been abandoned by the Noble One (*ārya*) and no longer manifests.

Second, due to forgetfulness, [the conceit] manifests abruptly; because of the presence of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and so forth, up to not having well-cultivated the Noble Path, the co-nascent conceit of self (*sahaja-māna*) still arises even while one is practicing.
Although they have severed the conceptual view of a self,
they still proceed because of their own latent tendencies and because they have not yet fully cultivated the Noble Path.

Regarding the statement that "the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), being constantly pursued by its latent predispositions (vāsanā), serves as the basis for the conceit 'I am' (asmimāna) at times of forgetfulness, causing it to arise momentarily," there are two interpretations of "latent predispositions" (vāsanā).
First, the gate of conformity:
even for noble ones (ārya), there remains the habitual tendency (vāsanā) of the conceptual view of self;
therefore, in conjunction with the conceit to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya-māna), it serves as the basis from which the conceit "I am" (asmimāna) arises.
The second explanation holds that the innate view of self (*sahaja-ātma-dṛṣṭi*) constitutes the habitual tendency (*vāsanā*).
It is called a "habitual tendency" because it arises based upon the conceptualized view of self (*vikalpita-ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, as for the noble ones who contemplate common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*),
if these noble ones were to contemplate the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
such as the solidity of earth;
Even when [contemplating] that wind is of the nature of motion and so forth, pride does not manifest in me;
how much less so when contemplating the common characteristics such as suffering and selflessness?
Regarding the statement, "If one attains even a momentary manifestation [of wisdom] concerning conventional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*),
etc.," it means that if one maintains right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) toward conventional phenomena such as jars or basins, my pride (*māna*) will likewise not arise.
If, regarding conventional phenomena, one does not abide in right mindfulness yet conceives of a real self and so forth, and the pride of "I" manifests;

furthermore, if within the continuum of a noble one (*ārya*), the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) of the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) have been entirely severed.
Discriminative views and pride have already been abandoned.

It is said that within the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) still persist and have not yet been permanently severed; this refers to those cases where the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) of the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*) have not yet been permanently severed.
This refers to the innate views and conceit (*sahaja-dṛṣṭi-māna*).
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "those who reckon themselves as desiring" is a general explanation of the scriptural text.
Master Bei also said:
"Regarding the statement that the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) consists solely of its latencies (vāsanā),
the Tripiṭaka Master offers two interpretations."
One [teacher] says: "This is the innate (*sahaja*) *anuśaya* of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Question:
"If that is so, why was the seed of the conceptualized (*vikalpita*) view of self previously called an *anuśaya*?"
Is the seed of this innate view of self called "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*)?
Answer: Because the seeds of the conceptualized [view] are powerful, they are termed "latent dispositions" (*anuśaya*).
Because these innate seeds are weak,
they are called "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*).
This is the second interpretation.
Regarding the introductory statement, "by means of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)," this refers to the seeds of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
As for what is here called "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*), it is as follows:
Or rather, it refers to the residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the conceptual view of self (*parikalpita-ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Because of these habitual tendencies of the conceptual view of self,
they can serve as the basis for innate self-conceit (*sahaja-māna*).
The Master Da said:
"It refers to three locations.
The first is the location of the view of 'I' and 'mine'."
Second, the basis for the discriminated *asmimāna*;
third, the basis for the innate *asmimāna*, and so forth.
Eighth, the explanation of the two kinds of consolation.
This refers to the third of the three types of questions and answers (*vyākaraṇa*).
Regarding the statement, "One should know that this question occurs among the four stages," it means that within the inquiry concerning *sukhāvatī*, there are four questions.
These may be understood by correlating them respectively with the four stages.
Regarding the ninth [section], the "Explanation of What Resembles the True Dharma":
herein, first, a sutra is cited to briefly distinguish the view of what resembles the true dharma.
Regarding the section beginning with "Furthermore,
there are two causes," the following provides a detailed analysis of the causes that give rise to views resembling the True Dharma (*saddharma*), according to their specific meanings.
Within this [section]:
Master Jing said:
"The general meaning is that both the heterodox and orthodox schools together interpret the statement in the sutra as saying that arhats do not comply [with the teaching]."
Furthermore, because there is ignorance regarding the objects [of experience] and so forth,

it is called "non-conformity. This refers to not knowing, as it truly is, whether one's engagement with food, activities, the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases in the present life is conformable or non-conformable.
Next, the false meaning is raised as an objection against the correct meaning:
it is said that the Arhat’s non-conformity is not "non-conformity" [in the true sense], for it is an irrational, false discrimination; it is not that the Arhat is non-conforming in the present life.
He himself explains this, saying:
"Why is that? Because those [actions], such as the preparation of food, are perceptible in the present."
It cannot be said that this is inconsistent with the present life;
rather, the statement in the sūtra regarding "inconsistency" has a distinct intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
For this reason, when Arhats pass into parinirvāṇa, they do not perceive or cling to the formations (*saṃskāra*) as being inconsistent.
To claim for oneself, "I say that my births are ended, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished,
and there will be no further existence," while not having properly understood future matters and so forth, is contrary to the teachings of the Sūtras.
The righteous masters below distinguish between what is correct and what is not;
therefore, it is said: "One should know that this is a semblance of the True Dharma.

Seeing that views arise through the power of two kinds of conditions, one should exert extreme effort for the sake of fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*) or great *śrāvakas* who wish to eradicate these views of a semblance of the True Dharma, so as not to allow those people to demonstrate them to others.
The Master Da says:
First, he correctly cites the scriptural text to explain the "non-conforming" (asādhaka) phrase regarding the Arhat;
second, from the words "the Arhat" onwards [is the explanation].

The Master of Treatises explains that "not in accordance with the truth" (asunyata) means that even Arhats possess ignorance regarding certain matters; because they do not discern and know the aggregates and elements of food, it is called "not in accordance with the truth."
Ignorance is also termed "non-conformity.
Regarding the Master’s explanation of non-conformity, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the meaning of non-conformity by those who do not hold the correct doctrine;
second, the section beginning with "It should be known that this is a semblance of the True Dharma," and so forth.
The proponents of the orthodox school explain this as being contrary to the intended meaning.
Within the explanation provided by the proponents of the heterodox school,
the first section interprets the scriptural text.
2. From "By this cause and condition" onwards, it clearly demonstrates the non-attachment to phenomena as objects of cognition.
3. From "Therefore, the World-Honored One" onwards, it cites a sūtra to establish the invalidity of the [opposing] position.
The Master said:
"An Arhat is not one who lacks knowledge of phenomena;
for what is presently visible—such as 'this is food,' 'this is clothing,' or 'these are the aggregates and elements'—is known by them."
Therefore, there is no clinging.
The proponents of the Correct Meaning (Zhengyi) refute this, saying:
"When an Arhat abandons this body, they enter the nirvana without remainder."
In what sense is it clarified that after its cessation there is neither non-attachment nor attachment?
This can be understood by consulting the commentary of the orthodox school (*siddhāntavādin*).
"By way of two kinds of meaning" refers to this.
First, do not allow that person to confess their own [faults] or fall into the most wretched destinies.
Second, out of love and reverence for the Buddha’s teachings,
do not cause the doctrine to become obscured or extinguished because of such views that resemble the true Dharma.
For these two reasons,
in order to eliminate that which resembles the True Dharma,
the second section extensively analyzes, according to their meaning, the causes that give rise to views resembling the True Dharma.
This section is divided into three parts.
First, it presents two causes that give rise to views resembling the true Dharma.
Second, it clarifies that two types of true Dharma are taught in order to sever those two causes.
The subsequent section clarifies that there are two faults regarding the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) that has not yet been abandoned.
Regarding the second provisional [teaching], it says: "In order to abandon these two causes, two true dharmas are taught.
The first is the true dharma of impermanence.
The True Dharma of the two kinds of selflessness is called the remedy for one cause,
or it universally remedies both causes.
Regarding the phrase "among the four turnings," etc.:
Master Jing said:
"The four propositions— namely, that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa there is the conditioned, the unconditioned, both, or neither—
are called the four turnings."
Master Tai said:
"The four phrases, beginning with 'conditioned,' clarify the progression;
therefore, they are called the 'four turnings.'"

Regarding what I have called "śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and Buddha-Bhagavats," you should know that these are two kinds of conventional designations: they are designated as conditioned within the state with remainder, and designated as unconditioned within the state without remainder.
The Arhats of the three vehicles,
when considered in their universal sense, are all called Tathāgatas;
for they have come by means of the path of reality to achieve perfect enlightenment.
However, within the state with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*), a conditioned self (*saṃskṛtātman*) is provisionally established;
within the state without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*), an unconditioned self (*asaṃskṛtātman*) is provisionally established.
Hereafter, these are negated from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
If it is said that, according to the ultimate truth, it is neither conditioned nor unconditioned,
this is because true nature is like an illusion, being produced through conditions;
thus it is said to be neither unconditioned nor conditioned.
Thus, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) should be without reality and not arise, being like a flower in the sky;
since both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned are unattainable,
how can one apply the five provisional selves (*pañca-prajñapti-ātman*) to them?
Through the teaching of such a Dharma instruction, when awakening arises in six aspects, one should know that views resembling the true Dharma are permanently severed.
First, there is the awakening to impermanence as it is subsumed within its basis.
Second, one awakens to this suffering within the present life;
third, one awakens to its spontaneous cessation as cessation—
this refers to the spontaneous cessation of the remaining karmic retributions of an Arhat.
Fourth, one perceives the realm of abandonment as cessation;
fifth, one perceives the realm of detachment as coolness;
sixth, one perceives the realm of extinction as final subsiding.
If one possesses such attachment to the extremes of conceptual proliferation,
one should rebuke that attachment which reckons that an Arhat, after his passing away, does not understand that future births of a self have been exhausted.
The tenth section, "Dispelling Doubts Regarding the Locus.
Master Jing says:

Within the internal laws and teachings, even regarding one who records [the realization of] non-arising (*anutpāda*), the Buddha constantly rebukes the arising of views of existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that at the end of life a disciple may perceive birth or non-birth,
and the further claim that there is a supreme, eternally abiding self— even as previously described—
the preceding passage stated that two subsequent causes can give rise to such views that resemble the true Dharma.
First, one has not yet permanently severed the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) within;
second, based on this, one falsely postulates a person (*pudgala*) who undergoes the process of transmigration and cessation.
To sever these two causes, the two types of true Dharma are taught as their respective remedies.
That is to say, one sequentially explains that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and selfless;
and within the four modes of turning, one thoroughly investigates and finds that a person (*pudgala*) who undergoes the process of transmigration or its cessation is entirely non-existent.
This refers to [the self] being based on the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and so forth.

Regarding the statement "due to two causes and conditions... up to because it is dissimilar," it means that the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) conceive of a self as existing, yet they find it impossible for such a self to be sovereign over what is directly perceived.
Therefore, the nature of selflessness is easy to understand.
Nevertheless, these formations (saṃskāra),
though devoid of a self, subsequently undergo seeing, hearing, sensing, cognizing, performing actions, and receiving retribution.
Each is distinct;
within this selflessness, it is furthermore difficult to comprehend its intrinsic nature.
Thus is the self-nature of this selflessness.
Its essence is profoundly deep;
its characteristics are subtle;
it appears as if profoundly deep.
The Master Da said:
"Regarding the mention of two types of locations,
the first refers to those from the Buddha downward."
The first clarifies doubt regarding the Buddha;
the second, from "Furthermore, having explained the ultimate truth" onwards,
clarifies doubt regarding the true dharma (*satyadharma*).
First, regarding those who harbor doubts toward the Buddha: why did the Blessed One,
the World-Honored One, denounce both the view of existence and the view of non-existence,
yet still provide a specific prediction concerning the death and passing of his disciples?
After his passing, will you record that one person has attained birthlessness (*anutpāda*) or that another has not?
Second, regarding the doubt concerning ultimate reality (*paramārtha*),
the non-Buddhists raise this objection:
If the ultimate truth cannot be apprehended within the present or the future,
for what reason do the masters of the Three Treatises (Trairāśika) assert that it exists?
As for the statement, "Although this characteristic is easily understood," [it refers to the following:]
The disciples of the Buddha-Dharma can easily understand the characteristics of impermanence and non-self;
therefore, it is said that they are "easily comprehended.
However, as for those whose characteristics do not correspond [to these], [it is otherwise].
The non-Buddhists do not understand impermanence and selflessness;
therefore, they do not resemble the Dharma.
One should know that from this point onward—
The eleventh [section] explains the non-annotation of alternative names within the sūtra;
the twelfth explains transformation and decay.
This may also be understood according to the text.
Thirteenth, the explanation of the Great Master’s prophecy:
it is said that "knowing this within the treatise on the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the abandonment of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) refers to the Tathāgata."
This is the preceding discourse on the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of these various graspings.
Furthermore, if these various graspings have not been abandoned, one perceives that they entail three kinds of disadvantages.
If there are three merits and so forth once [the afflictions] have been severed and extinguished,
this constitutes the second discourse on the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the severance of these various graspings (*upādāna*).
The fourteenth [chapter] explains the fulfillment of the three views.
The fifteenth [section] explains the characteristics of external delusion;
this may be understood according to the text.
The sixteenth [section] explains the establishment of the six divisions.
This refers to the first of the three gates subsumed by the final word "etc. (ādi) in the verse;
it constitutes the sixteenth gate in the prose commentary.
As for the "six divisions":
The character "yòu" (又) serves as a separator.
The seventeenth section explains the two types of treatises;
this constitutes the second gate within the "Inclusive Summary" (*saṃgraha*).
The eighteenth [section] explains the distinction between the two types, the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*).
This is the third gate within the aforementioned [group of] terms.
Regarding the "five characteristics":
Thus, the three unsurpassed [refuges] constitute the first three;
contemplating the Buddha-body is the fourth;
and serving the Tathāgata is the fifth.
2. Section on the Selection and Compendium of Matters in the Sūtras (Vol. 89, Part 1–Part 2). Regarding the fourfold interpretation of the sūtras mentioned above:

Regarding the statement that the fifth distinct factor is established by way of the meaning of contact (*sparśa*) as the fruit of the conjunction of the three: [it refers to the fact that contact is established based on that same conjunction].
Master Jing said:

Therefore, it is said in general that contact is the fruit resulting from the conjunction of the three.

As for the statement that the seventh and eighth members are established as two distinct categories based on the meaning of the two types of defilement—karma and afflictions (*kleśa*)—it is as follows:
The seventh distinct category of volition (*cetanā*) is established on the basis of the meaning of karmic defilement (*karma-saṃkleśa*);

Third, the explanation of ignorance (*moha*).

The nature of folly refers to that which, by way of entanglement (*paryavasthāna*), constitutes forgetfulness regarding the present life.
The manifestation of ignorance (*avidyā*) is termed "entanglement," while its inherent obscuration is termed "forgetfulness."
Regarding the phrase "by means of the latent dispositions (anuśaya), it is that which is destined to be lost":
this means that because the latent dispositions exist, they are capable of producing the future dharma of the loss of mindfulness through ignorance.
As for the expression "the establishment of the five aspects of experience": [it refers to the following].
This refers to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth as explained above.
The fourth [point], the absence of delusion,
is as stated in the text.

The sixth [section] provides an extensive analysis of liberation;

The fourth question and answer distinguishes the essence of liberation.
Regarding the first part:
it is as in the case of hearing, reflecting, and so forth, in accordance with reason.

Next, regarding the state of liberation, there are two [aspects].
First is the learner (*śaikṣa*),

Third, furthermore, there are five qualities by which a bhikṣu practicing mental purification accomplishes much;

First, regarding correct instruction, there are three kinds of true friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

This refers to obtaining three kinds of verbal instructions according to one's desire,

This means relying on three types [of practices] to increase fewness of desires and contentment; these are precisely the first three of the noble lineages.

Regarding "the instruction on the three [factors] for abandoning hindrances and tending toward love," this refers to the following.
One remains far removed from all hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), as well as from all dogmatic views (*dṛṣṭigata*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
There are three kinds of verbal instruction:

Since the first two instances of the explanation regarding the removal of hindrances already included that which coexists with the hindrance of ignorance (*avidyā-nīvaraṇa*),

Based upon that, one perceives superior qualities and deeply perceives the faults and disadvantages of the various formations (*saṃskāra*) within the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and their respective bases.

Seventh is the detailed analysis of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Depending on other sources, the afflictions may be analyzed through twenty-two doors or four doors.

All afflictions of the form and formless realms, excluding ignorance, are termed "outflows" (āsrava).

Based on meditative concentration, one becomes free from desire.
Apart from these two types of ignorance within the bodies of non-Buddhists,

Regarding the statement, "In those three realms, up to the establishment of the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*)," this means that the ignorance within the three realms present in the bodies of other persons is called the outflow of ignorance.

Excluding the ignorance arising from non-Buddhist paths,

As for the four, five, or six [factors],

Those based on cultivation not encompassed by skillful means are established as the two views constituting the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*).
"These distinctions constitute the three" refers to the summary of the three previously established [afflictions], such as doubt and so forth.
"The seventh is the occurrence of the fetter of lack of resolute conviction regarding the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya."

Regarding the eighth point, the matter of the poverty of wisdom in the chapter on renunciation:
it is the envy of others who surpass oneself.
Not bestowing the Dharma leads to ignorance and darkness in future lives;

As for the ninth basis, the matter of the poverty of wealth among those belonging to the householders' class,

It says: herein, because the mind is corrupted by envy, one gives rise to stinginess regarding the Dharma within the true Dharma;
by this, there will be a lack of wisdom in the future.
The third explains the three bonds (*bandhana*),

since this text is complete,

while it is not stated that those belonging to the class of renunciants within the True Dharma also give rise to various forms of grasping?
The following passage resolves this doubt:

because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, frequently declares of himself, "I am the one who has fully known and eternally severed all grasping," those who vow to practice this Dharma [should follow him].
Although they possess afflictions and their bodies perish at the end of life,
they do not establish any grasping therein,
because they have gone forth from home without any lingering attachment to sensual desires.
Therefore, one has no desire to grasp at views, precepts and observances, or the doctrine of self.
Because there is no grasping, there are no other three types of clinging.
There are two kinds of those who preach the Dharma poorly.
First, those who give rise to disputes based on views and craving;
second, those who are able to enter worldly meditative concentrations.
Based upon these disputes regarding views and craving, the grasping at views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa) is established.
Based on those who are able to enter worldly meditative concentrations,
the grasping at rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is established;
based on these two categories, one clings to the discourse of self (*ātman-vāda*).
Therefore, based on the category of the "conjoined" (sahagata), the grasping to the expression of self (*ātmavādopādāna*) is established.
Herein, "views" refers to the sixty-two views and those below;
this sets forth the nature of that which is grasped (*upādānīya*).
That which is maintained by false conceptual views is called "precept" (śīla);
the manifestation of dignified deportment is called "vow" (vrata).
Because it is based on [the notion of] truth and because one abides [in that view], the treatises describe the assertion of a self as "discourse on self" (ātmavāda).
This passage refers generally to both the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and the self that is conceptually constructed as the objective sphere of the grasping at a self (*ātmavādopādāna*).
Furthermore, within this context, "grasping for sensual desire" (*kāmopādāna*) is established with sensual craving (*kāmatṛṣṇā*) as its condition. Below.

it means that one gives rise to craving toward a conceived self—whether as existing or as non-existing—and this is termed the grasping at the doctrine of self.
The tenth section clarifies the four fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Those established solely based on non-Buddhists are still the same as the four bonds (*bandhana*).
The latent tendency of craving for the three realms is the first bond;
hatred and views pertaining to the desire realm are the second;
and the grasping at views pertaining to the three realms is the third.
The grasping at precepts and observances within the three realms constitutes the fourth bond.

The eighth section is the "Extensive Analysis of the Gates of Karma.
This text is divided into three parts;
the first clarifies the karma of the three evil realms.
Next, the two treatises on the heterodox and the orthodox are cited to demonstrate their differing explanations of karma;
the third section provides a detailed exposition of sixteen types of karma.
These first two segments of the text are contained in this fascicle.
The latter section appears at the beginning of the ninetieth fascicle.
Regarding the first three types of unwholesome courses of action (*akusala-karmapatha*),
the statement that "all unwholesome bodily actions are called misconduct (*duścarita*), and the same applies to speech and mind," refers exclusively to their nature as karma.
Unlike the Hīnayāna, which generally includes greed, hatred, and wrong view— these three mental factors— among the "evil conducts" (duścarita),
[the Mahāyāna] holds that regarding the various evil destinies (durgati), one has either already attained them, will attain them, or is currently attaining them, and so forth.
It clarifies that the three types of unwholesome conduct result in rebirth in the miserable realms, whether already attained or otherwise.
Next, it explains the establishment of karma and affliction through the two doctrines of the heterodox and the orthodox;

the repeated arising of intentional volition during the preliminary stage (*pūrvaprayoga*) with the desire to carry out killing and so forth is termed "intentional action" (*saṃcetanīya*).
Karma of this kind certainly leads to rebirth in the evil realms;
the *Abhidharma* refutes it.
According to your judgment, you would be slandering those who practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and are capable of realizing *nirvāṇa*.
Why is this? Because among all classes of sentient beings, when they create evil karma in the present life,
there is none who does so without having intentionally formed the thought to do it.
How much more so in other lifetimes?
This constitutes karma created through intentional reflection that will certainly lead to rebirth in the evil destinies;
thus, there would be no time at which liberation could be attained.
As stated in the *Nyāya-śāstra*,
those actions performed solely through intentional reflection are for the most part indeterminate (*aniyata*).
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says:
All sentient beings have more indeterminate karma and less determinate karma;
for this reason, there is the cultivation of the Path.
Determinate heavy karma can be made to be experienced lightly;
indeterminate karma is not to be experienced in a future life.

To clarify the correct doctrine:

it is said that if one intentionally performs unwholesome karma with full awareness, such karma is both performed and accumulated, and one will certainly experience its result in the miserable realms; whereas if there is karma that is performed but not accumulated, [one does not necessarily experience its result].
Because they rely upon the experience of various phenomena,
whatever actions are performed— whether or not there is subsequent regret, whether or not an antidote is cultivated,

whether experienced upon rebirth or in subsequent lives.
