Furthermore, this contradicts your established tenets such as "created by past karma" and so forth;
this is called the first fault.

Moreover, you state that all unwholesome dharmas have evil karma from previous lives as their cause; if this were definitively the case, then all wholesome dharmas would likewise have to arise spontaneously from wholesome dharmas of previous lives as their counterparts, and the cultivation of various counteractive measures would become entirely useless.
This is called the second fault.
Furthermore, if one fails to perform what ought to be done in the present,
and if all such actions were determined solely by past karma without depending on present conditions, [then this fault would follow].
There would be no present deliberation regarding what is wholesome that ought to be done or what is unwholesome that ought not to be done, and so forth;
furthermore, knowledge of reality as it is would become useless, insofar as one would already have realized: "I should turn away from this evil" and "I should accomplish this good."
Since he asserts that present conditions do not exist, this "self" must likewise be non-existent;
thus, the principle of knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūtajñāna*) is not established.
Because such knowledge is not established, the subsequent arguments presented in succession fail.
This is always the third fault.
Regarding the explanation of the five characteristics that constitute non-defilement,
Master Jing said:
If one posits a "person" as the experiencer, then this person is able to experience by virtue of the six bases of contact;
they are able to experience by relying upon the six sense faculties.
Regarding the fourfold distinctions within the mother's womb, up to the point of entering the womb:
This clarifies the method of entering the womb;
however, the fourfold distinctions within the womb have not yet been analyzed.
These fourfold distinctions will be set forth below.
That is to say, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling;
it is in this sequential order that there is an experiencer.
This differs from the minor treatises, which hold that contact and feeling occur outside the womb.
Now, it is explained that contact and sensation also exist within the womb;
these are the two truths subsumed under defilement,
namely, suffering and its origin.
That which is contrary to this, from "inferior" down to "pure," refers to the cessation and the path.
Regarding "feeling born of contact with clear [knowledge]":
Because "clarity" (*vidyā*) penetrates both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
The treatise states that there are three stages of clarity:
first, that which exists in the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), specifically within the seven preparatory practices (*prayoga*) prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The second is that of those in training (śaikṣa),
and the third is that of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Here, we clarify that the contact intended by the statement refers to the untainted (anāsrava).
The following conclusion states that there are thus the three truths of purity, cessation, and the path.
Master Da says:
"If one is able to receive [this teaching]..."
The five aggregates constitute the first characteristic.
If one experiences through these,
it constitutes the second by way of the six bases of contact.
If one experiences it in this way,
then name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact,
and feeling constitute the third [link] in such successive order.
Regarding the time of experiencing [the results]:
the experience of the two types of karma—past and present—constitutes the fourth [time].
Thus is defilement; thus is purification.
The two types of persons— those who are deluded and those who have attained awakening— are the fifth.
One should know that the phrase "herein, based on the five aggregates of clinging," and so forth,
explains the first line.
"Furthermore, this conventional person [is established] by means of the six contacts," etc.,
explains the second phrase.
"The fourfold distinctions within the mother's womb," etc., [explains the third phrase].
The third phrase is explained:
"Furthermore, this very sensation also functions in the present," and so forth.
The fourth phrase is explained.
Regarding the phrase "if they hear various incorrect dharmas," this explains the fifth clause;
there is yet another interpretation.
First, that which experiences;
second, that by which it experiences;
third, the manner in which it experiences.
Fourth, such is defilement;
fifth, such is purification.
These are the five characteristics.
The fourth pair clarifies the faults and benefits of the wrong and right practices regarding the establishment of phenomena.
First, the false treatises are distinguished;
subsequently, the correct treatises are elucidated.
Furthermore, regarding the preceding section,
it should be understood that the designation of "purity through wrong action" refers to the non-Buddhists' reckoning that ascetic practices can purify all past unwholesome karma.
It is said that he views the various unwholesome karmas of past lives as having two kinds of causes;
namely, that present unwholesome karmas are all induced by the habitual tendencies of past karma, and so forth.
Within the Buddha-dharma, there are also unwholesome states pertaining to the present life.
Due to past habituation,
it is subsequently aroused by present conditions;
that [consciousness] perceives only one [object].
Therefore, it constitutes a heterodox treatise.
"The Great Master having passed away" refers to the Buddha having passed away.

For what reason should it be understood that it is unreasonable to establish such [a state] as purifying karma, up to the point where, because of being oppressed by the three types of painful sensations, they cannot arise? Etc.
Furthermore, for example, when you cauterize your body with fire,
the fire is above,
while the heat is among the sufferings.
Fire is slightly bitter when ingested;
thus, these three types of suffering arise from present conditions.
Your claim that they arise from the past is illogical.
To claim that one can eliminate those three fires and three sufferings through ascetic practices is unreasonable. In brief,
the essential meaning is as follows:
That which is called the determination of the intrinsic nature of various karmas,
the determination of their timing,
and the determination of their categories.
Master Jing said:
"Furthermore, to speak of 'horizontal carving' is to name it 'determination' (niyata).
Master Da said:"
This is explained according to the single aspect of the conventional gate of following along.
If one relies on the gate of ultimate truth,
it is not necessarily so, because [the mind] can also arise simultaneously with them.
The following clarifies the main treatise.
As for the statement "analyzing the six matters," these are the four great elements, space, and consciousness.
Because one analyzes the phenomena of sentient beings by means of these six elements,
it is said that "those five kinds of distinctions,

which are contrary to them and praised by others," refer to what is praised by others as being contrary to the two types of false doctrines and the three types of practices involving self-inflicted suffering mentioned previously.
The fifth pair clarifies those who have not yet entered and those who have already entered the Noble Teaching.
First, regarding the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has not yet entered the Noble Teaching:
by means of three kinds of knowledge, one knows that [certain phenomena] cease and do not arise.
This person has already attained right view;
subsequently, upon hearing false teachings,
wrong view is about to arise and right view is about to perish.
Later, upon hearing the true teaching,
the arising of wrong views is called "abandonment" because they do not arise;
the prior establishment of right view is not called "arising."
Next, there is birth without cessation;
this refers to the person of the Middle Way,
who was previously neither heterodox nor orthodox.
Later, upon hearing the true Dharma, right view arises;
because this is called the arising of wrong view and its cessation through non-occurrence, it is not termed "abandonment.
Next, there is that which both arises and ceases.
This person previously held wrong views;
by hearing the true Dharma, those wrong views were suppressed and extinguished, and right view arose.
Second, there are three characteristics of those who have already entered the Noble Teaching and are still in training (śaikṣa).
It arises and does not perish.
This means that while on the stage of cultivation, when the four types of unshakable confidence (*aveccappasāda*) manifest, it is called "arising.
Regarding the Buddha, one does not speak of them as being of the same class [as other objects].
When entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), [defilements] are first abandoned;
at this present stage, they are not yet termed "extinguished.
Next, there are those that are extinguished and do not arise again.
That is to say, the cessation of the remaining categories of ignorance— which are to be abandoned through cultivation— is what is meant;
the essence of clear knowledge itself is not termed "arising."
Because it accomplishes that category,
next there is both arising and ceasing;
namely, the arising of the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga).
Because ignorance, which is to be abandoned through cultivation, has been completely extinguished.
Third, even ordinary beings who have already entered the holy teaching possess three characteristics:
first, they cease and do not arise.
This means that although one hears of non-self and thereby eliminates the view of self,
because one has not yet directly awakened to and entered into the right view of non-self,
it is not called "arising."
Second, they arise without ceasing.
This person, according to what was previously heard,
gradually becomes able to enter into the principle of selflessness through the right view of selflessness.
It is called "arising";
as long as the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) have not been abandoned,
it is not called "cessation."
From this point onward, through the power of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga),
one realizes the clear observation of the truths (satyābhisamaya) and thereby severs the latent tendencies (anuśaya), giving rise to the untainted (anāsrava).
This is then termed "both arising and ceasing."
In the ninety-first fascicle, within the extensive analysis of the categories of karma (*karmadvāra*) presented above,
the first two sections have been completed.
From here on, the third section provides a detailed explanation of the sixteen types of karma.
Among these,
first the sixteen categories of activity are listed,
and subsequently they are explained in sequence.
Within the preceding section, there are again two parts.
First, one half-verse indicates sixteen categories;
these consist of five pairs.
Thus, these five kinds of two-gate systems and thirteen [kinds] constitute ten kinds of three-gate systems.
Now, the preceding [fifteen] have the four types of karma as their final element; the four karmas,
such as the black and so forth, constitute the sixteenth.
The prose section should be understood as corresponding to the sequence of the verses.
Next, in the sequential exposition,
the five kinds of two-gate classifications are first explained.
It is said that karma becomes grave due to three causes and conditions: first, regarding the action of intention,
it refers to performing evil deeds with extremely intense fetters,
or performing good deeds with a purely pure mind.
Second, by way of application (*prayoga*),
meaning performing that action repeatedly and without interval;
third, by way of the field (*kṣetra*).
This refers to those who have been kind, such as one's parents;
and those who abide in right practice,
namely the four candidates for the fruits of the path.
Regarding the results of correct practice,
these consist of the four fruits of spiritual realization as well as Buddhahood and so forth.
This refers to performing wholesome or unwholesome deeds toward those who have been kind and toward the field of reverence.
Regarding the statement that "all karma within the continuum of one who is completely purified is called non-progressive":
for a person in training (*śaikṣa*), wholesome and unwholesome karma within their body does not increase.
Among the karmas created through intentional thought,
there is confusion: for instance,
intending to kill King A, one mistakenly kills Person B.
Although it is not killing as a karmic path,
it is nevertheless an action performed with volition; thus,
for one who is not confused.
That which is as previously described is what is intended;
that which is contrary to this is called "not intentionally committed" (akāmataḥ kṛta),
and is determinate karma (niyata-karma).
Thus, heavy karma created through intentional thought is both performed and increased;
whereas light karma created through intentional thought that is not subject to indefinite timing of its maturation is performed but not increased.
Karma created unintentionally is not considered here, as it is easily understood to be indeterminate.
Karma whose maturation has already ripened refers to karma that has already received its retribution;
the opposite applies to that which has not yet ripened.
Regarding the passage beginning with "If one wishes to realize arhatship," [the text] examines whether the two vehicles can act as obstacles.
Master Jing said:

Regarding the claim that when one is about to realize arhatship, previously committed karmic actions of fixed retribution (niyata-karma) act as obstacles because their ripened fruit (vipāka-phala) manifests,
this is like the karma that acts as an obstacle within the body of an ordinary person in training (śaikṣa), which is like the ocean or a mountain.
This refers to karma that results in a female body, birth in Uttarakuru, the Unconscious Heaven (*asaṃjñisattva*), or as a eunuch (*paṇḍaka*), and so forth.
Such karma can only act as an obstruction, preventing one from attaining arhatship, once it has manifested its fruit through rebirth.
These are precisely what are called karmic obstructions and retributive obstructions.
If they have not yet projected their fruit, they cannot act as obstructions;
therefore, it is said that they do not follow along with the continuity of the body.
Why is this? As for the statement that "it cannot even act as an obstruction":
if one has created karma to be experienced in a future birth during a previous life, one will experience the fruit of that karma in this body and will not attain arhatship.
If one has created karma in a previous life that is to be experienced in a subsequent life,
it cannot act as an obstacle to this present body; even if it does not act as an obstacle, [one] has already attained arhatship.
Nevertheless, it is not the case that this is not karma to be experienced with certainty. Why?
Because it is precisely based upon those afflictions, their concomitants, and so forth.
Master Tai said:
"That which is definitively unwholesome karma is called a karmic obstruction;
it can induce a body of diseased, unbalanced four great elements."
Illness occurs because the retributive fruit has manifested;
that the body composed of the four great elements cannot attain its fruit is termed an "obstruction of karma" (*karmāvaraṇa*).
It is not called an obstruction of karma because the seeds of karma follow after the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) within the body.
If this body does not receive the karmic retribution for deeds that obstruct the Path,

then although there may exist within the bodies of humans and devas the seeds of unwholesome karma with fixed retribution in a subsequent life, these cannot obstruct the attainment of the supreme fruit of Arhatship.
By this, it is shown that even within the body of one who has realized the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), there still exist evil karmas;
it is not that these cannot obstruct the attainment of the fruit of no-more-learning.
At the time of attaining the fruit of no-more-learning, one does not attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
However, those [karmas] that receive the name "definite karma" (niyata-karma) are so called because they rely on the presence of afflictions (*kleśa*) which act as auxiliary conditions for the karma.
Furthermore, because the continuity of the body is accompanied by afflictions in various states of existence,
karma that is definitely experienced is established;
for within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), there are no afflictions.
All karma that is to be experienced in subsequent lives and so forth is transformed so as not to be experienced at all.
According to the tenet of this treatise, this refers to those who are about to sever the afflictions, even regarding such karmas as the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*).
These are also subject to transformation;
this differs from the illustrative analogies which state that all things are subject to transformation.
Next, the ten kinds of threefold gates will be explained.
To speak of "thoroughly knowing according to reality" refers to skillful means; therefore,
it is called "wholesome."
Karma conducive to pleasant feeling consists of the wholesome karma of the first three dhyānas and that of the desire realm.
Karma conducive to painful feeling...
This refers to karma that can induce rebirth in the miserable realms (*durgati*).
The meaning of "karma not exhausted in the lower [realms]" is clear from the treatise itself.
Furthermore, there is also karma that induces pleasant sensations even among ghosts (*preta*) and animals (*tiryagyoni*).
Briefly stated, it is not clarified that the gods and humans of the desire realm also possess karma that induces painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanīya-karman*),
nor karma that accords with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukhavedanīya-karman*),
such as all karma belonging to the fourth dhyāna and the stages above it.
Question:
Is there the retribution of the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) below the third dhyāna?
Explanation:
The ālayavijñāna exists throughout all five destinies,
whereas the six consciousnesses are not fixed; regarding this,
the two masters of the Western Regions differ in their views.
One teaching states that from the third dhyāna downward, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) does not experience the retribution of equanimity (upekṣāvedanā).
This feeling exists only at the moment of birth and death;
according to the ālayavijñāna, which undergoes the experience of death and birth, the mental consciousness cannot exist at that time.
If one follows this interpretation in accordance with the text of this section,
it is only from the fourth dhyāna upward that there is the retribution of mental consciousness associated with equanimity.
The second master says:
Various treatises debate whether the third dhyāna and those below it possess [the ālayavijñāna] or not;
this debate concerns whether the *manovijñāna* abandons its retribution or not, but they do not debate the *ālayavijñāna*.
It is for this reason [that the following is stated].
The mental consciousness of the lower stages also involves the relinquishing of the life-force at death and the undergoing of rebirth;
this contradicts the present text.
We shall now reconcile these points.

This is stated merely with reference to the distinction between the three types of feeling (*vedanā*) across different levels; thus, it is said that the lower levels possess the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
In reality, however, both wholesome and unwholesome [karmas] can result in the retribution of equanimity.
This extends even to the final moment of life in hell and the moment of rebirth, where there is also the feeling of equanimity induced by unwholesome karma.
Regarding karma to be experienced in the present life up to karma performed at the time of action:
with the exception of the three types of retributive karma and the karma of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) or that of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*),
other karma cannot be specifically identified by its characteristics or modes of activity.
Such karma may result in retribution in the present life or in the next life;
this can only be stated in general terms as being rare.
As for the phrase "the performance of the ritual action":
This refers to the establishment of gifts and so forth.
If such characteristics arise because the various karmas one has performed have ripened as maturation (*vipāka*) within this present life,
it is as described regarding loving-kindness, the absence of conflict, and cessation.
One who has seen the path and one who is beyond training receive formal prediction from him;
the donor obtains the fruit,
which will be known in a future life.
Regarding the statement, "The karma of those in training (śaikṣa), up to and including the subsequent attainment (pṛṣṭhalabdha) of wholesome contaminated (sāsrava) karma, etc.":

this text refers exclusively to the uncontaminated (anāsrava) threefold karma and the wholesome contaminated karma within the person of a noble one (āryapudgala) who is still in training as being termed "training" (śaikṣa).
This is based on the definitive system of tenets.

In other texts, the wholesome factors of the stages conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), as well as the untainted (*anāsrava*) karma of the paths of seeing and meditation, are also collectively termed "training" (*śaikṣa*).
This is stated as a general definition based on similarity.
Regarding "the karma of one beyond training" (aśaikṣakarma) up to "the various karmas as appropriate":
all three types of untainted (anāsrava) karma and the three types of tainted wholesome (sāsravakuśala) karma within the continuum of one beyond training constitute the karma of one beyond training.
The remaining karmas are termed "neither-learner-nor-non-learner" (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
These comprise the karma of the three natures within the bodies of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana),

the unwholesome and obscured-neutral karma within the bodies of learners (śaikṣa), the non-obscured-neutral karma within the bodies of non-learners (aśaikṣa), and those that belong to neither category.
If it is said that karma associated with afflictions abandoned through seeing is called "karma abandoned through seeing," then by the same logic,
one should also say [it includes] the karma for the eighth existence, the karma of a female body, the karma of Uttarakuru, the karma of the non-percipient gods, and the karma of eunuchs and so forth.
These are all abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
"Karma that is not to be abandoned" refers to all supramundane karma of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Elsewhere there is a textual passage stating that ten elements (*dhātu*) are called "not to be abandoned," namely: the seven mental elements (*citta-dhātu*), and the elements of visible form, sound, and mental objects (*rūpa-śabda-dharma-dhātu*).
In this context, only supramundane training and untainted karma are designated as "uninterrupted.
This is because, by their very nature, they are truly uninterrupted;
whereas that [designation] refers to the fact that within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), all dharmadhātu have been severed and all fetters exhausted.
Therefore, it is called "uninterrupted. Question:
If that is so, and if that which has already severed its fetters within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is called "uninterrupted," [then what of others?]
This means that within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), all eighteen elements (dhātu) have already been completely severed and exhausted, which is termed "non-interruption" (anuccheda).
The commentary explains:
in principle, they are indeed equal.
However, because the ten realms possess the nature of goodness, they receive the designation "uninterrupted";
whereas the five faculties and three objects, being neutral by nature,
do not receive the designation "uninterrupted."
Regarding the statement "severed in the present life," this refers to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has not yet attained freedom from desire and dies while remaining in that state.
Such an ordinary person who is not free from desire first intentionally creates karma, but then gives rise to revulsion and suppresses it so that it does not proceed.
Having died while still not free from desire, one is reborn in that same stage;
yet, one is unable to ensure that such karma will not be created at the point of the subsequent birth,
nor that its maturation (vipāka) and so forth will not be experienced.
Although one may feel revulsion toward the karma created in the present life,
one cannot thereby prevent that reviled karma from drawing forth its retribution in the next life;
nor can one ensure that no further karma will be created within the body of that subsequent birth.
Nor can it ensure that no further karmic actions will be performed in subsequent states.
As for the statement that "even in the present life, one cannot invariably prevent the commission [of such acts]," this means that although the body may temporarily suppress what is being done,
[it does not guarantee total cessation].
Nor is it necessarily able to prevent that very same body from creating [karma] again.
As for the phrase "because it is severed at birth," this refers to the state subsequent to liberation, wherein one still performs actions and experiences their maturation (*vipāka*).
An ordinary person detached from desire, weary of the karma created in the present life,
is reborn in a higher realm at the end of their life;
thus, there is no body born in the desire realm in a subsequent birth for them to create karma within.
However, these ordinary persons later regress and are reborn;
because they previously cultivated karma through aversion to desire, they receive its subsequent retribution.
Within that body of subsequent retribution, they again perform karma.
Therefore, it is said that even after not yet being liberated, one performs karma in subsequent states and experiences its maturation.

Regarding the phrase "because it is subsequently severed," this refers to another case where there is one who, though still a learner (*śaikṣa*), has not yet attained freedom from desire for the desire realm; having already attained revulsion and having obtained either the first or the second fruit of śramaṇaship, he reflects: "Whatever evil karma I have performed, which was characterized by much heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) and much burning affliction..."
Alternatively, one may wish that all virtuous karmas be experienced simultaneously with them,
and not experience their retribution in a subsequent lifetime.

Having made this vow, one further cultivates the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*) and correctly applies the practice of meditative concentration belonging to the category of calm abiding (*śamatha*).
By subduing the afflictions, one attains the dhyāna of the future;
furthermore, it is for the sake of progressing toward the transcendence of sensual desire.
One should know that within this context, the intentionality of anger is severed by loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Harmfulness is the abandonment through compassion;
envy is the abandonment through long-life;
and desirable objects and the like are the abandonment through equanimity.

All karmas that have been performed are the very offspring of the mind; even up until the attainment of the fruit of non-returning, if one merely gives rise to joy and pleasure therein for a moment, or even at a later stage, [the result follows].
If one were merely to find temporary contentment in this fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) and not seek the higher fruit,
one would still not create karma in the present life such that one would be reborn again in the desire realm.
How much more so in the state after birth, where one is able to perform karma?
Furthermore, regarding those outside the True Dharma who have fallen into wrong views—all such persons are said to possess "crooked karma.
The wholesome and unwholesome karma arising within the bodies of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) is born from wrong views.
All are termed "crooked karma" (*vaṅka-karman*).
Regarding the statement that "all karmas arising from intense greed and hatred are termed 'defiled karma' (*kliṣṭa-karman*)," according to the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*,
these are precisely crooked karmas.
Furthermore, the karma arising from those [afflictions of] greed and hatred is collectively termed "defiled karma.
The phrase "those with violent delusion" refers to persons who create turbid karma.
"Those of superior grade with dull faculties who lose mindfulness" refers back to the aforementioned crooked karma;
"those who are extremely dark and dull-witted" refers back to the aforementioned defiled karma;
"karma produced by delusion" clarifies that it is karma created out of ignorance.
All of these are turbid karmas; they consist of the two types of karma—crooked and defiled—as well as those produced by delusion, along with turbid karma itself.
This is explained and distinguished in the *Vyākhyāyukti* (The Determination of Explanations), where it is treated differently from the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Regarding the statement that "all excellent conduct capable of leading to the happy realms is called pure karma":

according to the *Kṣudraka-śāstra*, all excellent conduct is subsumed under the three types of pure karma—both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)—as well as the three types of excellent conduct consisting of non-attachment and the other [wholesome roots]. Thus, they are collectively termed the "three excellences" and the "three purities."
In this present text, only the three types of tainted karma (*sāsrava-karman*) that lead to rebirth in the fortunate realms of humans and devas are termed "pure karma" (*śukla-karman*).
Furthermore, these are exclusively of the nature of karma and do not extend to what is non-karma.
The "action of silence" refers to all skillful practices that lead to nirvana;
this is precisely the action of the three perfections (*tri-pāramitā*).
As the *Kṣudraka-śāstra* states:
Regarding the perfection of the body and speech of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as the mind of one beyond training:
according to the force of the present passage, all sublime practices capable of leading to nirvāṇa are termed "silent karma" (*tūṣṇīṃ-karman*).
One should know that the three types of action— both with and without outflows— are all subsumed under the category of silent action.
Below, the four types of karma, such as the black and so forth,
which can induce rebirth in distinct locations, are explained.
The evil karma of the *lokā* is called "black-black" karma (*kṛṣṇa-kṛṣṇa-karma*).
In other texts, it is stated that all unwholesome karma is termed "black-black" karma.
Wholesome karma that brings about rebirth in the various distinct celestial realms is called "white-white" karma.
As stated in the following passage, above the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin) there is the palace of Māra;
wholesome karma pertaining to the regions above that palace, as well as the two higher realms, is called "white-white" karma.
Other sources state that all wholesome karma within the three realms is called "pure-white" (*śukla-śukla*).
As for the karma that can induce various results elsewhere being called "black-and-white" (*kṛṣṇa-śukla-kṛṣṇa*),
this refers to the six heavens of the desire realm, the four continents of human beings, as well as hungry ghosts and animals.
The wholesome and unwholesome karma that is reached [by this] is called "black-and-white, black-and-white.
In other texts, it is stated that the wholesome and unwholesome karma of the desire realm is called "black-and-white karma. Question:
Why are the upper and lower [categories] not the same?
The explanation says:
while the name is derived from a single meaning, in other contexts, four types of karma are established based on their specific functional natures (*karmasvabhāva*).
Therefore, it is said that wholesome [karma] within the three realms is called "white-white.
All unwholesome karma is called "black-black.
If one performs a mixture of wholesome and unwholesome deeds, it is called "black-white" or "white-black"; or there may be that which is black in intention but white in its preparatory application.
There may be actions that are black in their underlying intention but white in their skillful means;
such mixed karma is called "black-and-white.
If it is purely wholesome and unmixed with evil, it is called "white-and-white."
That which is purely evil and unmixed with good is called "black-black.

In this present text, the realms are explained in terms of retribution: the hells receive only the fruits of unwholesome karma, while from the palaces of Māra upwards, one receives only the rewards of wholesome karma.
In the interim, one experiences a mixture of suffering and pleasure;
therefore, based on this principle, the three types of karma are distinguished.
[The interlocutor] asks:
One might ask: since the palace of Māra is subsumed under the desire realm (kāmadhātu), could it possibly lack painful sensation (duḥkhavedanā)?
The explanation is:
even if painful sensation were present there, it would be a transformational (nirmāṇika) sensation rather than a retributive (vipākaja) one.

It is said that because from that place, the forms seen by the eye up to the phenomena known by the mind are exclusively desirable, characterized by continuity, excellence, and predominance, they are produced through the mental door and thus have the sense of being "mentally produced" (*manomaya*).
They are called "distinct" because they experience suffering individually and experience happiness individually.
The phrase "constantly experiencing through the gateway of the six bases of contact" means that one constantly experiences through the gateway of the six sense faculties.

In the explanation according to the topical divisions (*sthāna*), the first half-verse lists four gates: first, "establishment" (*vyavasthāpana*) and so forth; next, "equality of wisdom" (*jñānasamatā*) and so forth; and finally, it should be known that "detachment from desire" (*vairāgya*) and so forth.

In the prose commentary,
the first section explains the absence of wisdom.

First, crooked karma arising from wrong view;
second, defiled karma arising from greed and hatred;
third, turbid karma arising from delusion.
Furthermore, it arises with ignorance as its root.
If one can sever this root of non-self—the single dharma that gives rise to all defilements among all sentient beings—[then liberation is attained].
This explains the fundamental meaning.
This refers to the single phenomenon of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Among these, the first is the impairment of reality through the defilements that arise therein.
The first is wrong view.
The second, which superimposes unreal things,
refers to greed and hatred.
Third, regarding those who are deluded about the skillful means for manifesting reality as it is:
"because those who perform turbid karma are deluded regarding those two causes," and so forth.

Regarding the second explanation, the gate of wisdom consists of two kinds of knowledge in accordance with reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*):

The first two refer to the wisdoms arising from hearing and reflection;

Third is the explanation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Contemplating impermanence:

Those who do not rely on the four characteristics, but instead rely upon the false view of a self (*sakkāya-diṭṭhi*) to harm the four types of modes of conduct and arrogance, are the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Within a single aggregate (*skandha*), they reckon that "form is the self," "form belongs to the self," "form is the self's ornament," "form is the self's servant," and "form is the self's dwelling."
Based on these four meanings, the four types of conceit arise;
once one does not give rise to the four kinds of self-view regarding each individual characteristic,
one thereby destroys the four types of conceit.

Regarding the statement that, "due to the power of the predominant influence arising in accordance with conditions, the seeds for future existence in the present life may increase or decrease," this refers to the increase [of those seeds] when one contemplates dependent origination in its forward order (*anuloma*).
To contemplate in reverse is to observe diminution.
Through these forward and reverse contemplations, one observes whether future existence will arise or not;
this is precisely the contemplation of the two conditions of defilement and purity.

therein exists only the absence of the nature of "mine."
Furthermore, regarding this emptiness as the ultimate resort:
this unconditioned emptiness generally refers to the emptiness of the nature of persons and phenomena as they are conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*).

As for the dependent nature (*paratantra*), which consists of phenomena existing by way of causes and conditions, it takes as its ultimate resort the absence of any determinate, inherent principle (*dharmatā-yukti*).
Regarding the phrase "this may be thus, up to the principle of the nature of things (*dharmatā-yukti*)," Master Jingtong says:
"This may be thus according to the principles of the Mahāyāna."
This means that emptiness is identical to dharmas.

there are some non-Buddhists who reckon that emptiness and phenomena are neither different nor not different;
the following concludes this point accordingly.

the eighth [topic] explains the two kinds of abiding in emptiness;

it is said that "this existence and non-existence are ultimately and completely transcended.

Because there is no self, there is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

From here below is the second section, which clarifies the basis for the four kinds of emptiness.
